rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: The equations fail when acceleration changes with time.  ·  Area under a v–t graph is displacement, not acceleration.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: g is taken as 10 m/s^2 when the question asks for a simple number.  ·  A negative displacement means the body finished on the negative side of the origin.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: The three equations of motion apply only when the acceleration is constant. They are v = u + at, s = ut + (1/2)at^2, and v^2 = u^2 + 2as. Each symbol must be given a sign before it is used.  ·  On a velocity–time graph, constant acceleration is a straight line. The slope of that line is the acceleration, (v − u)/t, which rearranges to v = u + at.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: At the top of a vertical throw the velocity is zero, but the acceleration is still g downward.  ·  s in these equations is displacement along the line of motion, not necessarily the path length if the body turns back.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: The area under the velocity–time line is the displacement. For a straight line from u to v, the area is a rectangle ut plus a triangle (1/2)t(v − u). Using v − u = at turns that area into s = ut + (1/2)at^2.  ·  Eliminating t between v = u + at and the displacement equation gives v^2 = u^2 + 2as. This form is the one to choose when the time is not given and not asked for.  ·  For a body thrown upward, take upward as positive. Then u is positive, a is −g, and the velocity at the top is zero. The same equations describe free fall with u = 0 and a = +g if downward is positive.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Free fall  ·  Free fall uses a = g downward.  ·  Equations of Motion (Graphical Derivation) is based on fundamental principles.
